title: MZ Solo dev dark fantasy RPG in RPG Maker – looking for feedback on combat & ritual system

posts.author: SealDesk
posts.body:
Hi everyone,
I'm a solo developer working on
Requiem for Faith
, a dark fantasy JRPG built with RPG Maker MZ. The core gameplay loops are now solid, and I would love to get your valuable feedback on the combat mechanics.
Game Overview & Features:
Grim Gothic Setting:
Set in the fallen Kingdom of Varnath, where a failed ritual led to a demonic invasion of the capital city, Aurelia.
The Last Holy Knight:
Play as Seraphine, the sole surviving knight navigating the aftermath of a cathedral massacre.
Active Turn-Based Combat:
Tactical turn-based battles featuring timed parries and dodges to keep engagement high.
Ritual Skill System:
High-impact skills trigger "Ritual Minigames," requiring players to input specific rune sequences to maximize damage.
The project is under active development, and any feedback or constructive critique you can provide would be highly appreciated!
Thank you for checking it out!

posts.author: 3rr0r1n5ynt4x
posts.body:
The dodge/parry bar should not overlap with any other information on the screen, so it should not be positioned inside the status windows. It's probably difficult to find the perfect space to place it and the more I think about it the more arguments I find against many positions, but the current one is definitely wrong in my opinion.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Welcome to the forum!
Just a few thoughts from an old Zombie, so feel free to disregard.
It may be a design choice on your part, but I find the lack of ending punctuation in dialog and certain messages on the screen distracting and odd (just me being a Grammar Zombie).
The video was a bit too quick for me to really gauge how the timed block/parry bar works. It might be better to let it go back and forth a couple of times. Unless that isn't how it works and you only have one immediate try. In which case, I probably wouldn't like that too much.
The input runes mechanic seems fine, but it could get a bit tedious depending on how frequently it happens.
Now, just a thought about turn-based combat in general. Again, just personal perspective.
For me, I enjoy turn-based combat because it gives me time to consider what I'm doing without feeling rushed. And it allows me a break while actions are being taken. If I wanted to play a button mashing combat game, I wouldn't be playing a turn-based combat game.
So, the more you have that requires active player timed input, the more you are moving away from what makes turn-based combat appealing to some (but not all).
I'm sure there are a large group of players who like the hybrid model that combines turn-based and active timed input.
Just like there are players that prefer either all active input or all turn-based input.
For many, this probably wouldn't be a deal breaker if the rest of the game was fun and enjoyable. But, for me, I'd probably prefer straight turn-based with no mini active timed inputs.
Of course this also depends on how frequently the player engages with combat and the mini active input parts. For instance, if the required timed inputs only happen a couple of times in a combat.
I think it would also depend on what type of notice you get so the player isn't surprised and caught off guard.
I think an even better concept (if you can do it) is to make the timed input mechanic optional. Something you can turn off or on in the settings. That allows you to appeal to a wider audience.
Unless you feel strongly that the timed inputs are in integral part of the game experience.
I think this is something that might benefit from some repetitive loop testing. Meaning set it up where the player is engaging in combat continuously to see how you (and then play testers) feel about the active timed inputs after a few dozen combats.
The game looks nice though. I particularly like the style of the portraits and the mostly full character images. And maybe it's just me, but it does seem like the sprites are a little taller than the default chibis, but I could be wrong. I like taller sprites in general.
Anyway, good luck on your project and remember to enjoy what you do!

Thank you so much for the warm welcome and the detailed feedback! I really appreciate the perspective of an experienced player.
You bring up valid points about the hybrid mechanics. To put your mind at ease:
The Rune Command system only appears during 'Limit Break' attacks.
It won’t happen during normal attacks or skills, so it shouldn't interrupt the flow too often. Also, I completely understand the appeal of pure turn-based combat, so
players will have the option to skip or disable the Rune input entirely
if they prefer.
I'll definitely take a look at the punctuation and the parry bar speed as well. And you have a sharp eye—the sprites are indeed customized to be taller! Thanks again for the encouragement.

posts.author: lianderson
posts.body:
Looks good.
My only complaint is the munchkin sized heroes. (this is seen a lot in rpg maker games, as well as some bigger games like octopath) It's one of those bad graphical choices that's just generally accepted because some other games do it.
If you actually want to break from that mold and look amazing, there's a few solutions. One is to simply make the heroes larger, which does take a lot of work, but is work well spent.
Another is making enemies smaller, but zooming in the camera so they're a reasonable size to your current party sprites. (depending on how many enemies you have, this could ironically take even longer)
Either way, I highly advise looking into a solution of some kind. But if you're fine with the way it is, as a lot of rpg maker devs are, then forget this post ever existed.
Good luck on your game.

Thank you very much for taking the time to write such a thoughtful and honest piece of feedback. I really appreciate how clearly you explained your concern.
The point about “tiny hero sprites” honestly hits close to home. It’s something I’ve personally gone back and forth on, and you’re absolutely right that it has become an almost unquestioned norm in RPG Maker–style games, often more for practical reasons than for visual quality.
At the moment, I’m carefully weighing the solutions you suggested—either scaling up the heroes or adjusting enemy size and camera framing. As you said, both approaches are a significant investment of work, but also potentially very worthwhile if the goal is to truly stand out visually.
I can’t promise an immediate change, but I can promise that this feedback won’t be forgotten. My goal is to push the game beyond the “typical RPG Maker look” as much as possible, and comments like yours genuinely help guide those decisions.
Thanks again for the constructive advice and the encouragement. It really means a lot to an indie developer.
